summary: For 5–6 year olds learning to compare and group everyday materials by simple physical properties. The core objective is that children sort a real set of materials by a stated property, justify each placement with a property word, and — crucially — re-sort the SAME set by a different property to discover that groups depend on the chosen rule, not on a fixed identity of the object. Activities centre on hands-on sorting with real materials; a drag-to-sort surface, a tap-to-reveal illustrated sort, and a short categorisation check are included as complementary supports with their limits noted.
misconceptions: Believing a material has one fixed group, not realising the same set re-sorts differently when the property changes (a Patterns-concept hurdle).
Sorting by the object's identity or use (all the cups together) instead of by the stated physical property.
Grouping by irrelevant surface features (colour, size) rather than the chosen property.
Placing an item without a rule — grouping intuitively and being unable to justify it in property words.
Assuming a material can only ever be in one group, so an item that is both shiny and hard can't belong to two overlapping sorts.

activities.title: Sort real materials, then re-sort by a new rule
steps: Lay out a tray of real materials: wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric.
Choose ONE property and say the rule out loud before touching anything (e.g. 'see-through vs not see-through').
Sort every item into two hoops or trays, saying a property word for each placement ('I put the glass jar with the clear plastic toy because you can see through both').
Now sort the SAME items again, but pick a DIFFERENT property (e.g. bendy vs stiff, or hard vs softer). Notice which items move home.

Point out an item that changed groups and say why (e.g. 'the foil was with the wood for not see-through, but with the fabric and sponge for bendy'; the glass only leaves the plastic under 'hard' if the plastic toy is soft or squashy).

If you are ready, use two overlapping hoops labelled with two different properties (e.g. 'shiny' and 'hard') and put an item that has both, such as the metal key, in the overlap; an either/or pair like see-through vs not see-through or bendy vs stiff has no true overlap.
activities.insight: A group is not a fixed fact about an object; it depends on the property you choose to look at. The same material can belong with different partners under different rules.

activities.title: Same-and-different pair comparison
steps: Take just two materials at a time (e.g. glass jar and clear plastic toy; or wood block and metal key).
Say one property they SHARE ('both are hard' or 'you can see through both').
Say one property where they DIFFER ('the glass is see-through but the wood is not').
Record each in a 'same' column and a 'different' column, using property words.
Repeat with other pairs so comparing becomes a stepping stone into sorting a larger jumble.
activities.insight: Comparing two materials by naming a shared and a differing property is the bridge from describing one material to grouping many.

activities.title: Read a finished sort and explain each placement (illustrated support)
steps: Look at a completed transparent/opaque grouping of pictured materials.
Tap or point to any item to hear or say the property reason it sits where it does ('this is here because you can see through it').
Then look at the same items shown re-sorted by a new rule (e.g. waterproof vs absorbent) and notice which pictures moved.
Say which item changed group and why.
activities.insight: Each group follows a property rule, and the same items can be arranged differently under a different rule — reinforcing the vocabulary and hinting at rule-dependence.

activities.title: Drag-to-sort bench with a swappable rule (optional interactive support)
steps: Drag a jumble of pictured materials into two bins labelled 'transparent' and 'opaque' — glass and clear plastic to one side, wood and metal to the other — saying why each goes where.
Press a 'change the rule' control so the bins relabel to 'waterproof' and 'absorbent' and the items scatter, then sort the very SAME materials again.

Notice an item that genuinely changes partners — for example the metal key, which sat in the 'opaque' group with the wood but now joins the glass and plastic in the 'waterproof' group, while the wood (shown as bare, unvarnished wood, which slowly soaks up water) moves to 'absorbent'.

Use a 'both / not sure' zone for a borderline item, such as wood that soaks up water only slowly, and discuss it; for items that truly have two properties at once, use two non-opposite labels such as 'shiny' and 'hard' (for children ready to go further).
activities.insight: Switching the rule and watching the same set redistribute makes directly experienceable that groups depend on the chosen property.

activities.title: Quick categorisation and odd-one-out check
steps: Drag or place items into two property bins to show you can apply a single rule.
Answer an 'odd one out by property' question (which one does not belong, and which property makes it the odd one?).
Match a compare-pair: given two items, say the shared property.
For pre-readers, use pictures with spoken labels.
activities.insight: Children can demonstrate they sort by a single stated property and spot shared or differing properties.

checkQuestion: Put out a tray of materials (wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric). Say: 'Sort these into two groups using ONE property you choose, and tell me your rule.' Watch them do it. Then: 'Now sort the SAME things again, but pick a DIFFERENT property this time.' Watch whether they can re-group the identical set.
checkAnswer: Sorts consistently by a single stated property (e.g. see-through vs not), names the rule, then re-sorts the identical set by a different property (e.g. bendy vs stiff) — showing that the groups depend on the property chosen, not on fixed identities of the materials.
